name: unit-of-work
intent: Maintain a list of the objects affected by one business transaction and write their changes to the database in a single ordered flush, so that each business operation commits exactly once and in a consistent state.
problem: A business operation touches several objects, and writing each change as it happens produces many small database calls, keeps a transaction open for the whole interaction, and leaves the database inconsistent whenever a later step fails. Nobody can say which rows one operation will change, deletes and inserts arrive in an order the database rejects, and the same object is often written twice because two code paths each saved their own copy.
context: Domain or service code that modifies several related objects per business operation and must persist them atomically, against a store that offers multi-statement transactions. It applies once the decision 'when do my in-memory changes become SQL?' has to be answered in one place - typically behind a Data Mapper, Repository or Active Record layer, in request-scoped services, batch importers, or any code that must coordinate inserts, updates and deletes whose order the database constrains.
benefits: One commit per business transaction: every change the operation made is written together, so a partially applied business step never becomes visible to other readers.
Fewer database round trips: pending inserts, updates and deletes are batched and ordered instead of emitting one statement per attribute change.
The domain model stays persistence-ignorant: objects are mutated normally, and no setter contains SQL or knows when the flush will happen.

Change tracking is centralised: the register of new, dirty and removed objects is the single source of truth for what a transaction touched, which makes auditing, event publication and cache invalidation feasible.

Write ordering can honour referential constraints (inserts before updates before deletes, parents before children) - an ordering that ad-hoc writes get wrong in exactly the cases that only fail in production.
It is the natural place to integrate concurrency control: optimistic version checks or pessimistic locks are applied at flush time for every modified row at once.
Transactional behaviour becomes testable: the flush can be forced, inspected or discarded, and the same unit of work can run against an in-memory database.
tradeoffs: The register/flush machinery is real code: change sets, snapshot copies or instrumentation, ordering, and error handling for a flush that failed halfway.
Change detection costs memory and CPU - a snapshot per loaded object, or proxies/bytecode weaving, plus a diff of every tracked object at commit.
Flush ordering must be computed; a wrong order surfaces as foreign-key or unique-constraint violations at commit time, far from the code that caused them.
Implicit flush timing is hard to reason about: a query issued mid-transaction may flush pending changes first, producing surprising writes, extra round trips or deadlocks.
A unit of work that lives too long holds the database transaction (locks, MVCC bloat) and serves a stale in-memory view; keeping it request-scoped is a discipline the pattern cannot enforce.
After a rollback the in-memory objects still look changed; unless the unit of work is discarded and the graph reloaded, the next flush can write state that no longer matches the database.
It hides SQL: N+1 loads, missing indexes and lock contention become visible only under load, and debugging spans application code, mappers and the flush itself.

Concurrency resolution is not free: without an integrated version check or lock the pattern's promised resolution of concurrency problems is a claim rather than a behaviour, and the last writer silently wins.

In distributed systems, a Unit of Work scoped to one service cannot atomically commit changes that span multiple databases - it coordinates local commits only; cross-service consistency requires patterns outside this catalog.

participants.responsibility: Registers objects as new, dirty or removed during one business transaction, keeps their identity, and at commit computes and executes the ordered set of statements inside a single database transaction.

Application or service code that creates, mutates and deletes domain objects and hands them to the unit of work - explicitly, or implicitly through a session/context. It decides where the transaction boundary is.
The object being changed. It stays persistence-ignorant and does not know it is tracked, except where a version attribute supports optimistic concurrency.
Translates one registered object into the INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE statement for its table, including identity and foreign-key columns, so the unit of work never contains per-table SQL.
Optional but usual companion: one instance per database identity inside the unit of work, so registering the same row twice updates one object instead of creating duplicates or two competing writes.

use_cases: A web request or service call that must commit all of its changes together: create the order, decrement stock, append the audit row.
Batch importers and ETL jobs that load thousands of objects and must flush them in ordered chunks, committing once per chunk instead of once per object.
Aggregate edit screens where one user action changes a parent and several children, and the whole graph must be saved or none of it.
Domain services that orchestrate several repositories and must share one transaction and one set of pending changes rather than committing per repository call.
Test fixtures that build a graph, flush it inside a transaction and roll it back afterwards, so every test starts from the same database state.
Offline or mobile clients that collect local edits and replay them to the server as one transaction, with conflict detection at flush time.

Financial ledger operations: a double-entry bookkeeping entry requires debit and credit journal lines written together — the Unit of Work orders the inserts so the transaction is atomic and the balance invariant holds.

CQRS command handlers where one command touches multiple aggregates: the application service opens one Unit of Work, loads and modifies each aggregate root, and commits once — ensuring the command succeeds or fails as a whole.

Event-sourcing projections: a projection handler replays a stream of domain events to build read-model state; the Unit of Work batches all read-model writes into one flush at the end of the event-batch, making the projection idempotent and atomic.

Multi-tenant SaaS with schema-per-tenant isolation: each tenant request is wrapped in its own Unit of Work scoped to its schema context, preventing cross-tenant writes even when the same DbContext pool is reused.

Offline/mobile sync clients that collect edits locally, reconcile them against the server, and send one batched transaction — the Unit of Work detects conflicts at flush time using the version column.

Order placement with inventory reservation and payment processing: a single business transaction decrements stock, creates the order, and records the payment — all three must commit atomically or none should.
Multi-entity approval workflows: an approval action modifies a request entity, sends a notification entity, and logs to an audit trail entity, all in one flush.

Parent-child creation with database-generated keys: creating a parent and its children in one transaction where the parent's generated ID is needed to link the children — the Unit of Work defers the INSERT until flush and makes generated IDs available within the same transaction.

Bulk pricing updates: a price-change batch modifies hundreds of product entities; the Unit of Work collects all dirty entities and flushes them in one ordered batch at the end of the batch job, dramatically reducing round trips.

Cross-aggregate domain event handling: within one Unit of Work, a command handler loads aggregate A, applies a change that raises a domain event, the event handler loads aggregate B and modifies it — both aggregates are committed in a single transaction.

Multi-database writes in a single service: when an operation must write to two separate databases within one logical business transaction, the Unit of Work coordinates both DbContext instances, each with its own local transaction, while the application layer manages the final two-phase commit or compensating rollback.

Audit logging with the transactional outbox: domain events are captured in-memory during the Unit of Work, written to an outbox table in the same transaction as business changes, and a background relay publishes them after commit — ensuring events are never published for uncommitted state.

Doctrine ORM (PHP): EntityManager::flush() delegates to a literal UnitOfWork class that computes change sets against the identity map and executes a referentially safe commit order — inserts, then updates, then deletes in reverse commit order — inside one database transaction, with preFlush/onFlush/postFlush hooks around the sequence.

MikroORM (TypeScript/Node.js): the EntityManager implements Unit of Work with an identity map — em.persist() defers the INSERT and em.flush() computes change sets and writes them in one transaction; flush modes (COMMIT, AUTO, ALWAYS) decide flush timing, and a per-request forked EntityManager keeps exactly one unit of work per HTTP request.
avoid_when: The operation writes a single row: one statement inside a transaction is simpler than a register/flush mechanism.
The path is read-only: no register and no flush are needed, though an Identity Map alone may still be worth it.
The transaction would span human think-time or several requests: hold no database transaction across that gap - use Optimistic Offline Lock and re-validate at commit.
The store offers no multi-statement transactions (some key-value or document stores): the atomicity the pattern promises cannot be provided, only deferred writes.
A framework already ships the pattern and you would only wrap it: a second unit of work around EF Core's DbContext or a Hibernate Session double-tracks changes and splits flush timing.
The change is one set-based statement anyway (a single UPDATE ... WHERE ...): loading objects in order to flush them is slower than the statement itself.
Your workflow spans multiple services with independent databases: a local Unit of Work can only commit its own database; use patterns outside this catalog for cross-service coordination.
anti_patterns: Long-lived unit of work (session per conversation): a database transaction and a change set held across user think-time, blocking other writers and serving stale objects.
Wrapping a framework that already implements the pattern - a second unit of work over DbContext or a Hibernate Session - so two trackers disagree about what is dirty and when it flushes.
A unit of work that flushes on every registration: the batching, ordering and single-commit benefits are gone and only indirection remains.
Sharing one unit of work across threads or coroutines: change sets, connections and identity maps are not thread-safe.
Using the unit of work as a cache and serving objects from it after commit or rollback instead of discarding or reloading them.
Silent lost updates: registering and flushing with no version check or lock while claiming the pattern resolves concurrency problems.
saveAndFlush inside @Transactional (or equivalent): forcing a flush mid-transaction re-introduces per-object round trips, defeating batching; use save() and let the transaction commit flush once.

Propagation.SUPPORTS on a write method: when called outside an existing transaction the writes auto-commit independently; if the second write fails the first is already committed — use Propagation.REQUIRED.

Mixing read and write SQL inside a Unit of Work without understanding AUTO-flush: a JPQL query mid-transaction flushes all dirty entities first, causing premature writes, unexpected locks, and constraint violations from partially-formed entities.

Long-lived Unit of Work across user think-time: holding a session open across multiple HTTP requests keeps a DB transaction, holds locks, and grows the identity map with stale objects — use optimistic offline lock instead.
Repository calling SaveChanges internally when using Unit of Work: repositories that call flush or save inside themselves break the atomicity guarantee — only the Unit of Work should call commit.

Registering repositories separately from the Unit of Work: if IRepository and IUnitOfWork are both registered and resolve to different DbContext instances, changes in one are not visible to the other — the Unit of Work must own all repositories.
Flush inside a loop: calling uow.flush() inside a for/foreach loop emits one database round-trip per iteration instead of batching all changes into one commit.

Holding a database transaction open across external I/O calls (HTTP, message queue): the transaction holds a connection and any row locks for the duration of the external call — use the Transactional Outbox pattern instead.

Using the Unit of Work to span multiple databases without a coordinating two-phase commit: each local Unit of Work commits independently; if one commit succeeds and another fails, the system is left with partial state visible to other readers.
design_principles: Single responsibility: one component registers changes, one maps objects to statements, one owns the transaction boundary.
Separation of concerns: domain logic mutates objects; the decision when and in which order they are written belongs to the unit of work.
Information hiding and persistence ignorance: the domain sees neither SQL, nor connections, nor flush timing.
Atomicity as a design invariant: one business transaction, one commit - partial business states must not be observable.
Open/closed principle: new entity types join through their mappers, not by editing the flush algorithm.
Dependency inversion: the unit of work depends on mapper and identity-map abstractions instead of concrete SQL.

One aggregate root per transaction: in DDD, only one aggregate should be modified within a Unit of Work; cross-aggregate consistency is achieved via eventual consistency and domain events, not wider transactions.

Transactions are an application-layer boundary: in clean architecture, the Unit of Work lives in the application or infrastructure layer, never in the domain layer, so domain logic remains testable without a database.
best_practices: Keep units of work short-lived and bounded by one business transaction - usually one request or one service call.
Register on every mutation path, or use snapshot/instrumentation tracking, so no change can silently miss the flush.
Order the flush deterministically: inserts, then updates, then deletes, parents before children, with the mappers supplying the SQL.
Never share a unit of work across threads or coroutines; give each concurrent task its own.
Discard or clear-and-reload the unit of work after a rollback instead of reusing objects whose changes were rolled back.
Pair it with Version Number or Optimistic Offline Lock so the flush detects conflicting writes instead of overwriting them.
Force a flush only where read-your-writes or an early constraint violation must be observed, and keep those points deliberate and few.

Flush ordering is not optional: inserts before updates before deletes, parents before children — a wrong order surfaces as FK or unique-constraint violations at commit time. Rely on the ORM's topological sort or implement an explicit dependency graph for custom implementations.

Pair the Unit of Work with optimistic locking (a @Version / rowversion column) so concurrent flushes detect conflicting writes instead of silently overwriting each other — without this, the pattern's concurrency promise is hollow.

Use the identity map consistently: every read of the same database key within one Unit of Work must return the same in-memory instance. Loading the same row twice through two code paths without the identity map produces duplicate objects, duplicate UPDATEs, or lost updates.

Prefer explicit flush points (commit, explicit flush call) over implicit AUTO-flush triggered by mid-transaction queries — implicit flushes cause surprise writes, extra round trips, and deadlock windows invisible until production.

When lazy-loading inside a Unit of Work, guard against triggering a flush mid-transaction: a lazy collection access may cause the ORM to flush pending changes before loading related data, producing writes the business logic never intended.

For async service layers, use an async-aware Unit of Work (e.g. EF Core DbContext with SaveChangesAsync) and avoid blocking calls inside a transaction — holding a DB connection across async I/O wastes the connection pool.
Keep one commit per business operation: if a service method calls SaveChanges or flush more than once, the transaction boundary is in the wrong place and partial states may already be committed.

Integrate domain event publication before the flush, not after: collecting events during the transaction and dispatching after commit ensures events are only published for changes that actually persisted.

Repositories must never call commit or flush: when the Unit of Work pattern is layered over an ORM, repositories should only register changes; the application service or use-case handler calls commit exactly once at the end.

Scope the Unit of Work to one logical transaction in DDD: modify only one aggregate directly; reference other aggregates by identity, not by object reference — cross-aggregate consistency is achieved through eventual consistency via domain events.

When an ORM already implements the pattern (EF Core DbContext, Hibernate Session, SQLAlchemy Session), wrap it in an explicit IUnitOfWork abstraction only when the application layer must not reference the ORM directly — otherwise the double-abstraction adds ceremony without value.

In EF Core, register DbContext as scoped lifetime and IUnitOfWork as resolving the same instance within that scope; never separately register repositories and the Unit of Work, as that creates two DbContext instances with independent change trackers.

For explicit transaction control in EF Core, use IDbContextTransaction — begin it before the first operation, commit after the last, and always rollback in a catch block or finally block to avoid leaving connections in an undefined state.

In Hibernate/JPA, prefer FlushMode.AUTO (the default) but understand its interaction with JPQL queries: AUTO flushes before queries that may read pending changes; use FlushMode.COMMIT to delay flush until commit when you know queries will not overlap with pending writes.

Batch size matters: configure hibernate.jdbc.batch_size (Hibernate) or EF Core's ChangeTracker.AutoDetectChangesEnabled strategically — batching reduces round trips but increases memory pressure in very large transactions.

In SQLAlchemy, the autoflush behaviour (flush before Query or Session.execute by default) can be disabled per-session with autoflush=False; disable it when you issue queries that you know won't read pending changes to avoid premature writes.
The Unit of Work is not a cache: after commit, discard or clear the unit of work rather than serving objects from it — stale objects cause subtle bugs that only surface in production.

Avoid holding a database transaction across external I/O (HTTP calls, message queue sends): the held connection and locks block other writers and can cause cascading timeouts under load; write locally and use the Transactional Outbox to relay events asynchronously.

When using SaveChangesAsync multiple times within one business operation, wrap the entire sequence in an explicit BeginTransactionAsync/CommitTransactionAsync pair so that a mid-operation failure rolls back all prior saves — without this, the first SaveChanges commits independently.

For bulk operations, batch the Unit of Work flush into chunks (e.g., every 500–1000 entities) rather than loading all dirty entities into memory at once; this controls memory pressure and keeps transaction duration short.

In Hibernate, prefer the graph-based ActionQueue (the default since Hibernate 6): it uses foreign-key and unique-key dependencies to compute a safe flush order automatically, unlike the legacy fixed-order ActionQueue.

Use FlushMode.MANUAL (Hibernate) or equivalent when you must control exactly when SQL executes: no automatic flush occurs, giving you full control over statement timing at the cost of potentially reading stale data.

In EF Core with retry-on-failure (EnableRetryOnFailure), wrap multi-step explicit transactions in CreateExecutionStrategy().ExecuteAsync(...) — a manually-started transaction cannot be retried automatically if the connection drops mid-flight.

The Saga Pattern: Distributed Transactions Without Two-Phase Commit (Usama Qamar, 2026) — Practical guide to saga vs 2PC; choreography for loosely-coupled steps, orchestration for explicit business workflows; compensation as semantic undo (not a database rollback); why transactional outbox is inseparable from reliable saga implementation; idempotency as a correctness condition. https://www.usamaqamar.space/writing/saga-pattern-distributed-transactions-choreography-orchestration

Saga Pattern Explained: Distributed Transactions for Microservices (Ajit Singh, 2026) — Outbox + CDC as the foundation of every reliable saga; idempotency keys for safe retries; choreography spiral problem leading to orchestration preference; dual-write problem and why outbox solves it; Chris Richardson's Eventuate Tram Sagas as the canonical Java library; Temporal/Step Functions as managed alternatives to custom engines. https://singhajit.com/saga-pattern-distributed-transactions/

System Design: Microservices Data Patterns (techinterview.org, 2026) — Dual-write problem as the fundamental issue the outbox pattern solves; polling vs CDC (Debezium) outbox relay; saga choreography vs orchestration decision guide; CQRS projections fed by saga events; anti-patterns of distributed transactions (2PC across microservices, synchronous chains, shared databases). https://www.techinterview.org/post/3233474197/system-design-microservices-data-patterns-saga-outbox-pattern-event-sourcing-cqrs-dual-write-problem-transactional-messaging/

Distributed Transactions: Saga, TCC, Outbox, and 2PC (Calmops, 2026) — Pattern comparison matrix by consistency guarantees, coordination style, and use-case fit; TCC with provisional holds; Saga for long-running BASE workflows; CDC-based Debezium outbox for near-real-time event publishing from the transaction log; durable execution platforms (Temporal, Step Functions) as saga alternatives. https://calmops.com/software-engineering/distributed-transactions-patterns-implementation/

Unit of Work: Redundant or Absolutely Essential? (NashTech Blog, Hoang Vo Huy, 2025) — SRP argument for why DI-scoped DbContext sharing is insufficient; Unit of Work as the sole commit authority preventing scattered SaveChanges calls; IUnitOfWork as an abstraction shielding the service layer from ORM coupling; constructor injection of repositories into UoW for shared DbContext instance. https://blog.nashtechglobal.com/unit-of-work-redundant-or-absolutely-essential-debunking-the-net-architectural-debate/

Unit of Work and Repository Pattern in EF Core: The Right Way (Rodrigo Bercocano do Amaral, Medium, 2025) — Why EF Core's DbContext IS a Unit of Work by design; DbContextFactory for background jobs and parallel reads only, never for coordinated writes; repositories must not call SaveChanges; one clear commit boundary per use case; manual transactions only needed for multi-step EF+ADO.NET mixed operations. https://medium.com/@rbercocano/unit-of-work-and-repository-pattern-in-ef-core-the-right-way-9f7e6a641415

Rethinking SaveChanges: Transactional Boundaries and Best Practices in Entity Framework (Ryan Xu, 2025) — Anti-pattern of multiple DbContext instances in one request (business data vs audit trail) leading to split transactions; Unit of Work + BackgroundService pattern for outbox-based audit logging; all SaveChanges calls eliminated from the service layer; one commit at the controller level for atomicity. https://oninebx.github.io/blog/backend/rethinking-savechanges-transactional-boundaries-and-best-practices-in-entity-framework/

Implementing Unit of Work Pattern in EF Core (Anton Martyniuk, 2024) — Practical walkthrough: IUnitOfWork interface with SaveChangesAsync; DbContext implementing IUnitOfWork directly; repositories adding to change tracker without calling SaveChanges; complete PlaceOrder use case with Order + Shipment as separate repositories committing atomically. https://antondevtips.com/blog/implementing-unit-of-work-pattern-in-ef-core

Mastering Data Access Patterns with Entity Framework Core 8 (DotNet Wisdom, 2025) — EF Core 8 improvements for data access; Repository vs Unit of Work vs direct DbContext decision guide; tracking vs NoTracking; compiled queries; batching; when to consider Dapper alongside EF Core for high-performance reads. https://dotnetwisdom.co.uk/2025-04-14/mastering-data-access-patterns-with-entity-framework-core-8/

Doctrine ORM Documentation: Unit of Work (current) — the UnitOfWork tracks all managed entities in an identity map keyed by root entity name, computes change sets against a stored copy of original values, issues UPDATEs only for changed fields, and determines insert/update/delete order at flush to maintain referential integrity; markReadOnly excludes entities from change-set calculation. https://www.doctrine-project.org/projects/doctrine-orm/en/current/reference/unitofwork.html

Doctrine ORM UnitOfWork source (current) — commit() dispatches preFlush/onFlush, computes a referentially safe order with the CommitOrderCalculator, begins a transaction, then executes collection deletions, entity insertions, entity updates, extra persister updates, collection updates, and entity deletions in reverse commit order before COMMIT, rolling back and closing the EntityManager on error. https://github.com/doctrine/orm/blob/master/lib/Doctrine/ORM/UnitOfWork.php

doctrine/orm issue #11345: UnitOfWork should run UPDATES and DELETES in a specific order (community, 2023) — UPDATE order follows hydration order rather than a deterministic key order, so concurrent flushes acquiring row locks in different sequences produce share-lock deadlocks; proposal to sort updates by entity type then id. https://github.com/doctrine/orm/issues/11345

MikroORM Documentation: Unit of Work and Transactions (current) — identity map inside the UnitOfWork returns the cached instance for repeated primary-key lookups; em.flush() computes change sets from original vs current values and executes them in one database transaction; flush modes COMMIT, AUTO (default) and ALWAYS configurable per ORM, EntityManager, QueryBuilder or query. https://mikro-orm.io/docs/unit-of-work

MikroORM Documentation: Working with Entity Manager (current) — only managed entities are tracked; em.persist() queues inserts and em.flush() executes computed change sets; detached entities are invisible to flush until re-attached with em.merge(). https://mikro-orm.io/docs/entity-manager

Django Documentation: Database transactions (current) — ATOMIC_REQUESTS wraps each request in a transaction (commit on success, rollback on exception) and transaction.atomic() provides atomic blocks with savepoints, but each model.save() emits SQL immediately: request-scoped atomicity without deferred change tracking, i.e. atomicity without a Unit of Work. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/topics/db/transactions/
